<note>The text above represents a library call number. In the Library of Congress system, "BV" refers to Practical Theology, with this specific range often covering books on Christian asceticism and mysticism.</note>

<term>Franciscan Order</term> <note>A Catholic religious order founded by St. Francis of Assisi in the early 13th century</note>, <term>Heraldry</term> <note>The practice of designing and displaying coats of arms</note>, <term>BV 5080</term> <note>The classification for works on the history and theory of Christian life and mysticism</note>, <term>Stigmata</term> <note>Bodily marks or sensations of pain in locations corresponding to the crucifixion wounds of Jesus Christ</note>, <term>Cross-bearing orb</term> <note>original: "globus cruciger"; a symbol of Christ's authority over the world</note>, <term>Library of Congress classification</term> <note>The system used by many research libraries to organize their collections</note>

**Description of the Central Emblem**

The center of the volume is adorned with a gold-stamped heraldic shield of the Franciscan Order. It features a central cross behind two crossed arms. One arm is bare, representing the arm of Christ, and the other is clothed in a sleeve of a religious habit, representing the arm of Saint Francis. Both hands display the **stigmata** <note>the sacred wounds</note>. Below these arms sits a **cross-bearing orb** <note>symbolizing the global reach of the faith</note>, and the entire shield is surrounded by a celestial field of stars.

# THE MIRROR OF SIMPLE
# SOULS <note>Originally titled in Old French as *Le Miroir des âmes simples*, this is a masterpiece of Christian mysticism. For centuries, its author was unknown, though it is now attributed to Marguerite Porete.</note>
<insert>✓</insert>

->*By an unknown French mystic of the thirteenth century*<- <note>The "unknown" author was Marguerite Porete (c. 1250–1310), a French Beguine who was executed for heresy. Her name was only rediscovered as the author in 1946, nearly twenty years after this edition was published.</note>

->*Translated into English by*<-
->M. N.<- <note>M. N. is the pseudonym of the 14th-century translator who translated the work from French into Middle English.</note>
->*Now first edited from the manuscripts*<-

->CLARE KIRCHBERGER<- <note>Kirchberger was a pioneering scholar of medieval spiritual texts who prepared this first modern printed edition.</note>

# INTRODUCTION

## MANUSCRIPTS AND TEXT

**T**HE <term>MIRROR OF SIMPLE SOULS<note>Originally written in French as "Le Miroir des âmes simples" by the mystic Marguerite Porete in the late 13th century. This book explores the soul's journey toward divine love.</note></term>, here for the first time printed, came to light in 1911, when Mr. J. A. Herbert, Keeper of <term>MSS.<note>An abbreviation for "manuscripts," referring to documents or books written by hand before the invention of the printing press.</note></term> in the British Museum, pointed it out to Miss E. Underhill, in a manuscript purchased for the British Museum at the Amherst sale (now MS. Adds. 37790). Miss Underhill wrote an account of the work which appeared in the *Fortnightly Review*, 1911, and published some extracts in No. 8 of the *Porch* in the same year. At a later date Miss Hope Allen discovered another manuscript in the Bodleian <note>The main research library of the University of Oxford.</note> (Bodl. 505), and a third in the Library of St John's College, Cambridge (MS. 71), together with a Latin translation made from the English version, by <term>Richard Methley of Mount Grace<note>A Carthusian monk and mystic (c. 1451–1527) based at Mount Grace Priory in Yorkshire; he was known for translating spiritual works into Latin for a wider scholarly audience.</note></term>, Yorks, <term>extant<note>Still in existence; not lost or destroyed.</note></term> in MS. 221 of Pembroke College, Cambridge.

Up to date no further English manuscripts have appeared, nor has any trace been found of the thirteenth-century French original of which the *Mirror* is a translation. <note>Though the author of this introduction notes the original French was lost, it was later identified in 1946 as the work of Marguerite Porete, who was burned at the stake for heresy in 1310.</note>

The three English manuscripts all belong to the

<summary>This page introduces the modern history of "The Mirror of Simple Souls," detailing its 1911 rediscovery in the British Museum and identifying the key surviving medieval manuscripts and their locations.</summary>
<keywords>manuscripts, J. A. Herbert, Evelyn Underhill, Richard Methley, Mount Grace, British Museum, Bodleian Library, Marguerite Porete, Middle English, Latin translation</keywords>

HEADER: INTRODUCTION

# INTRODUCTION

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the description of manuscript dates.</note> second third of the fifteenth century <note>Roughly between 1433 and 1466.</note>, and **Bodley 505** is almost contemporary with **MS. Adds. 37790** <note>The British Museum manuscript mentioned on the previous page.</note>, but the dialect is slightly more northern and retains some older forms. It appears also that the <term>scribe<note>A person whose professional job was to copy out documents and books by hand.</note></term> had access to an older <term>MS.<note>Short for "manuscript," a book written by hand rather than printed.</note></term> with different readings and occasionally additional matter, and these readings correct the British Museum version. Therefore the **Bodley MS.** has been chosen as the basis of this text.

The book is divided by all the scribes into long sections, approximately the same, but **Bodley** further subdivides into chapters, and in a late fifteenth-century hand there are added analyses of the subject-matter of these chapters, written on small scraps of paper and pasted in the margin opposite the capital letters which denote the chapter divisions. We cannot determine whether these analyses belonged to the earlier MS. of the book, but it seems improbable, for there is no indication of them either in the British Museum or Cambridge, or the Latin MSS. We have, however, retained them as affording a valuable indication of the general drift of the argument, and as elucidating the unpunctuated chaos of the British Museum MS.

The **Cambridge MS.** belongs also to the mid-fifteenth century. It is in a better hand than either of the others, and is both beautifully written and <term>illuminated<note>Decorated with bright colors, gold, or silver, often featuring intricate borders or small illustrations.</note></term>. It appears to

<summary>This page explains why the Bodleian manuscript was chosen as the primary source for this edition, noting its unique chapter divisions and helpful marginal summaries not found in other versions.</summary>

Three of these are in the Vatican, and it appears that they are translations from the *lost* French text <note>The original Old French version of "The Mirror of Simple Souls" was considered lost for centuries; the book was originally written by Marguerite Porete, who was executed in 1310.</note>, and differ considerably from Methley’s version made from the English translation. > ...[Ruys]broeck, who was prior of the Carthusian order and first composed this little book. <note>Original Latin: "...broke qui fuit prior de ordine cartusiensi et hunc libellum primo composuit." This is an erroneous historical note found in some manuscripts.</note>

By the middle of the fifteenth century, the works of the Flemish school were held in high repute among English mystics.

**Richard Methley** (born 1451) died as the vicar of **Mount Grace Charterhouse** <note>A well-preserved Carthusian monastery in North Yorkshire, known as a center for spiritual writing in the 15th century.</note> in 1528. He left, besides this work and his translation of the *Cloud of Unknowing*, a small autobiographical **work** <term>opuscule<note>A minor or short literary work.</note></term>, found in Trinity College, Cambridge, MS. 1160. It is a devout sketch of the daily life of the **Carthusian** <note>A silent, contemplative order of monks who live as hermits within a community.</note> monk, together with his own aspirations, fears, and experiences.

## THE MIRROR

THE MIRROR OF SIMPLE SOULS is a treatise of some 60,000 words, on the progress of the soul from the earlier stages of the spiritual life to its highest and rarest experiences. The treatment is didactic <note>Intended for instruction or teaching.</note> and psychological;

### THE FORM

The form derives, perhaps, from the verse <term>Jeu-Partis</term> <note>Literally "divided games"; these were medieval poetic debates where two performers took opposite sides of a question, often concerning love.</note>. These were verse competitions produced at the <term>Puys</term> <note>Medieval musical and literary guilds in France and the Low Countries.</note>, in which some question is mooted and alternate sides are taken by two or more characters. Generally the subject is proposed on one side, and the opponent chooses his argument and defends it on the humaner line of reasoning. The proposer takes the superficial rationalist and often satirical point of view, and at the end an appeal is made to the Judge of the Court, who sums up and solves the problem. Topical questions and allusions are frequent; the chief characters are often Love, Reason, Courtesy, and Joyful Thought <note>original French: *Amour, Raison, Courtoisie, Jolive Pensée*.</note>.\* The method is also that of the scholastic disputations at the <term>Sorbonne</term> <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, famous for its rigorous intellectual debates.</note>, and reflects the interest of a society delighting in <term>sophistry</term> <note>The use of clever but potentially misleading reasoning; here used to describe the era's love for complex intellectual puzzles.</note> and intellectual subtleties of every kind. To have applied this mode to the consideration of the mystical life, shows an ingenuity not altogether unworldly.

# INTRODUCTION

## THE AUTHOR

We cannot determine with any exactness who was the author of the *Mirror* <note>Original Latin title: *Speculum Simplicium Animarum*; a complex work of Christian mysticism.</note>, nor has anything further come to light since Miss Underhill <note>Evelyn Underhill (1875–1941), a renowned scholar of mysticism who first introduced this work to modern English readers.</note>, in 1911, conjectured that he may have been a secular priest <note>A priest who works in a parish among the public rather than living in a cloistered monastery.</note> or a Carthusian <note>A member of a very strict, contemplative monastic order known for their silence and solitude.</note> living on the borders of Flanders and France in the last third of the thirteenth century. He refers to a river, flowing through many countries, called the Meuse or Oise. This, together with the fact that two of the three censors to whom he sent his work belonged to the locality of Liège and Querayne <note>Likely modern-day Quiévrain on the Belgian-French border.</note>, and that the third, though a Master of Arts at the Sorbonne <note>The famous theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note>, was also a Canon of Liège <note>An administrative member of the clergy attached to a cathedral.</note>, and intimately connected with ecclesiastical affairs in that city, seems to establish the nationality of the author and the locality where the work was put forth.

<margin>🏹</margin>He was certainly in touch with the learned world of his day, deeply read in mystical theology <note>The study of the soul’s direct, experiential union with God.</note>, and experienced in questions of scholastic philosophy <note>The medieval method of learning that used Aristotelian logic to explain Christian doctrine.</note>. His chief sources seem to have been St Augustine, Clement of Alexandria, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>An influential early Christian theologian whose "negative theology" emphasized God as being beyond all human description.</note>, with the commentaries of the Victorines <note>Scholars from the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris, famous for combining academic rigor with mystical experience.</note>. He is greatly indebted to Richard of St Victor and to the author of the “Letter to the Brethren <note>original Latin: *Epistola ad fratres de Monte Dei*; a famous work on the contemplative life often attributed to St. Bernard but written by William of St. Thierry.</note>

The opinion of all these censors is to the same effect, that the book was sound theologically, but laid itself open to misinterpretation at the hands of superficial and unlearned men. Moreover, they agreed that the fair promises of so high a spirituality might lead the unwise to adopt a course more exacting in its claims than they could foresee, and to which, not being called by God, they should certainly never attain. The boldness and humour of the Fleming <note>Referring to the author, Marguerite Porete, who was from the County of Hainaut in the Low Countries (modern-day Belgium/France).</note> seems to have pleased his <note>The editor here uses masculine pronouns, though the author was later identified as a woman.</note> censors, and their verdict appears to have satisfied him. There is also an Italian translation.

The dangers which the thirteenth-century <note>The 1200s, the era when the book was first written.</note> critics foresaw, and against which they warned the author, were thoroughly fought out in the late fourteenth century, and again in the seventeenth century. It is possible that the French <term>MS.</term> <note>Abbreviation for "manuscript," a hand-written book or document.</note> reached England through the agency of a group of persons who accompanied Queen Philippa of Hainault <note>The queen consort of King Edward III, originally from the Low Countries (modern-day Belgium/Netherlands).</note> to England in 1327. # INTRODUCTION

There is a certain rhythm in this latter part of the work, found in the alternating descriptions of the condition of "free souls" and the condition of those who are "marred" <note>In this context, "marred" refers to souls that are spiritually hindered or stuck in their own self-will rather than being fully surrendered to God.</note>. A careful balance is maintained, even where the author tends to emphasize the poetic and lyrical aspects of the spiritual journey (similar to the final two books of *St. John of the Cross* <note>A 16th-century Spanish mystic and poet known for "The Dark Night of the Soul."</note>). Any contradictions in doctrine are only on the surface; they disappear if we remember the distinctions made earlier between the four (not three) classes of people: the perished, the marred, those living a life of spiritual affection, and those free souls who are united to God by love.

## AUTHOR’S SOURCES

Our author is clearly more influenced by Franciscan philosophy <note>A school of thought emphasizing the will, love, and the humanity of Christ, rather than just abstract logic.</note> than by the formal academic "scholasticism" of the time; he is a follower of St. Augustine and St. Bonaventure. What he owed to Dionysius the Areopagite <note>original: "Dionysius Areopagita"; an influential early Christian philosopher who wrote about the "Divine Darkness" and the limits of human language in describing God.</note> reached him through the Victorines <note>A group of philosopher-monks from the Abbey of St. Victor in Paris who focused on the heart’s role in reaching God.</note>. On the whole, he remains untouched by the "new scholasticism" that was being formulated by St. Thomas Aquinas, which had not yet come to dominate the thinking of the church schools. 

The main idea of his work is the glorification of love above intellectual knowledge; the immediate, felt knowledge of God is placed above rational reason. Goodness and a "good will" are valued more than academic learning. This perspective is carried to an extreme in his contemptuous attacks on that Reason which is merely "literal" <note>Meaning a rigid, intellectual understanding that follows the "letter" of the law or text but misses the living spirit.</note>, and in his praise of "not-knowing" and—

It is impossible to estimate the influence of the *Mirror* <note>Referring to *The Mirror of Simple Souls*, the book this introduction describes.</note> on that susceptible Flemish-Franco borderland in that age of spiritual fervour, the early fourteenth century. Certainly there are unmistakable points of contact between its teaching and that of the Brethren of the Common Life <note>A Roman Catholic pietist community in the Netherlands in the 14th century.</note>, Ruysbroeck <note>Jan van Ruusbroec, a Flemish mystic.</note>, Eckhart, Suso <note>Henry Suso, a German Dominican friar and student of Eckhart.</note>—even the Friends of God <note>original: *Gottesfreunde*; a medieval mystical group of laypeople and clergy within the Catholic Church.</note>. In England we can only hazard conjectures. # INTRODUCTION

## THE DOCTRINAL SIGNIFICANCE OF THE “MIRROR”

Certain points in the doctrine of the *Mirror* <note>Referring to the *Mirror of Simple Souls*, the mystical treatise attributed to Marguerite Porete.</note> call for special comment, in that they seem to contribute something to the history of <term>mystical theology</term> <note>The branch of theology that focuses on the soul's direct, personal experience of or union with the Divine.</note>.

First we take the “Far night,” the experience described by the <term>Areopagite</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian philosopher who taught that God is beyond all human understanding and can only be known through "unknowing."</note> as a dark knowing of God. This has been admirably analysed by Dom Justin McCann, in his Introduction to the *Cloud of Unknowing*, in this series. In view of this no further analysis is needed. I would only venture to add that, whereas the <term>Areopagite</term> represents the Darkness as a necessary mode of knowing God, to be attained by an elevation of the mind, laborious at times, the author of the *Mirror* regards the darkness as being of a temporary nature, arising when the spiritual life is well advanced, and being intermittent in its first approaches. To it he attributes certain <term>purgative</term> <note>The process of cleansing the soul of its attachments to the world and its own ego.</note> and <term>illuminative</term> <note>The stage of spiritual progress where the soul receives deeper understanding and enlightenment from God.</note> effects which become more marked as advance is made. Though he describes the ensuing complete passivity of the soul as belonging chiefly to the times of prayer, it would appear that, at the end of the journey, there is some sort of identification of the soul with “the gentle far night,” in its complete union with God (cf. Division XII, chap. ii).

<summary>This page explores the concept of the "Far night" in the Mirror of Simple Souls, distinguishing its intermittent and transformative nature from the more philosophical "dark knowing" described by Pseudo-Dionysius.</summary>

## INTRODUCTION

The reader will distinguish for himself its beauties and excellences, the happy originality of expression, the rare subtlety and depth of thought, and its spiritual elevation. It is not too much to say that, in this period, it is unique both in form and in content. None of the single English fourteenth-century **spiritual treatises** <note>Books or formal writings that discuss the principles and practice of the inner religious life.</note> cover the whole ground which our author treats systematically, yet not with that arid, methodical precision that mars much of the later spiritual treatises. The descriptive treatment is foremost and successful. In England the translation must have fallen between ***Rolle’s*** <note>Richard Rolle (c. 1300–1349), an English hermit and mystic known for his passionate, lyrical writings on the love of God.</note> work and that of ***Julian of Norwich*** <note>An English anchorite (c. 1342–1416) who wrote the first known book in English by a woman, focusing on God's love and mercy.</note>, and have been contemporary with the ***Cloud*** <note>Referring to "The Cloud of Unknowing," an anonymous 14th-century guide to contemplative prayer that emphasizes seeking God through "unknowing" rather than intellectual study.</note> and ***Hilton*** <note>Walter Hilton (c. 1340–1396), an Augustinian canon and author of "The Scale of Perfection," a guide to spiritual growth.</note>. Throughout, the method of English mystics is unsystematic, descriptive, and more suggestive than doctrinal, except in the case of Hilton’s *Scale of Perfection*. The *Cloud of Unknowing* comes nearest to the teaching of our author concerning prayer, but does not include in its range the variety of problems which underlie the teaching of the ***Mirror*** <note>The Mirror of Simple Souls, the text to which this introduction belongs.</note> and establish its value as a guide to the **interior life** <note>A person's inner spiritual life, characterized by prayer, reflection, and the relationship between the soul and God.</note>.

None of the single English fourteenth-century **spiritual treatises** <note>Instructional books or formal writings that discuss the principles and practices of religious life and the soul's journey.</note> cover the whole ground which our author treats systematically, yet not with that methodical precision that mars much of the later spiritual treatises. The descriptive treatment is foremost and successful. ## THE PROLOGUE

**T**HIS book, which is called *The Mirror of Simple Souls*, I—a most unworthy creature and an outcast among all others—many years ago translated out of French into English according to my modest skill <note>original: "lewd kunning" — in Middle English, "lewd" meant unlearned or belonging to the laity, while "kunning" referred to knowledge or ability.</note>, in the hope that, by the grace of God, it should benefit those devout souls who shall read it. This was truly my intention. But now I am moved to work upon it anew, because I have been informed that some words therein have been misunderstood; therefore, if God wills it, I shall explain those words more clearly. For though Love <note>Referring to the character of "Lady Love," the personification who acts as the primary teacher in this mystical dialogue.</note> explains those points in the same book, it is but briefly spoken, and may be taken in a way other than it is meant by those who read it hastily and take no further care. Therefore, if such words are explained a second time, they will be more accessible <note>original: "of audience" — here meaning profitable, understandable, or reaching a wider range of listeners.</note>,

# THE MIRROR OF [DIVISION I]

### PAGE 2

"...they shall misunderstand it, all those that read it or hear it."

Now listen with humility among yourselves, at the beginning of this, to a small <term>parable</term> <note>original: "ensample"; a story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual point.</note> of worldly love, and understand it as a metaphor for divine love.

There was in olden times a lady, who was a king’s daughter of great worth and noble character, who lived in a foreign land. It happened that this lady heard tell of the great courtesy and the immense <term>generosity</term> <note>original: "largesse"; the noble quality of being liberal and bountiful in giving.</note> of King Alexander <note>Referring to Alexander the Great, who was frequently used in medieval literature as the ultimate symbol of worldly nobility, power, and virtue.</note>; and she immediately loved him for his noble kindness and for his high reputation. 

But this lady was so far from this great lord, upon whom she had set her love, that she could neither reach him nor see him. Because of this, she was very often distressed, for no love but this one satisfied her; and when she realized <insert>[that]</insert> this distant love—which was so close to her heart—was physically so far from her, she sought to comfort herself by imagining some figure that might carry the likeness of the one she loved, for whom she felt her heart was so often wounded. 

And then she had an image painted that represented the king’s <term>appearance</term> <note>original: "semblance"</note> as closely as possible; and by the sight of this image, along with other practices, she was comforted. Thus she soothed herself through the representation of <insert>[that]</insert> love, by which she was <term>lifted up</term> <note>original: "updrawn"; a technical mystical term describing how the soul is pulled upward toward God by the force of desire.</note>.

# Ch. 3] SIMPLE SOULS

When a soul gives herself to perfection, she labors busily day and night to acquire virtues by the counsel of reason. She strives against vices at every thought, word, and deed that she perceives comes from them, and busily searches out vices in order to destroy them. Thus, the virtues are her mistresses, and every virtue makes her go to war with its contrary, which are the vices. The soul feels many sharp pains and a bitter conscience in this war.

These pains and sufferings exist not only in the exercise of the spirit—by putting away vices and gaining virtues—but they also come from bodily exercise performed by the commandments of the virtues and the counsel of reason: to fast and stay awake in prayer, to do penance in many various ways, and to forsake all her own pleasures and all desires and likings. In the beginning of all this, it is often very sharp and very hard. But she did all this by the commandments of the virtues, which were the first ladies and mistresses of this soul. She was subject to them all the while she felt this pain and war within herself. # CHAPTER IV

## CONCERNING CERTAIN THINGS THAT THE SOUL DOES NOT REGARD, HOW SHE IS LOST IN THE MOST HIGH THROUGH AN ABUNDANCE OF KNOWLEDGE, AND BECOMES NOTHING IN HER UNDERSTANDING, AND WHAT SHE ATTAINS THROUGH THIS

> "This soul," says Love, "does not care about <term>shame</term><note>shame: Here, the soul is so focused on God that she is indifferent to her social reputation or the judgment of others.</note> or honor, nor poverty or riches, nor comfort or discomfort, nor love or hate, nor even hell or paradise."

> "O Love, for God's sake," says Reason, "what is the meaning of what you have said?" 
> 
> "What is the meaning?" says Love. "Only those to whom God has given understanding know this, for no <term>Scripture</term><note>Scripture: While usually meaning the Bible, here it refers more broadly to any written religious learning or human study.</note> can teach it, nor can human intellect comprehend it. Neither the hard work of any creature nor human merit can reach it. “Ah, what can this be, Lady Love,” says Reason, “that this soul may will in this way—as this writing says—when it was said before that she has no will?”

“O Reason,” says Love, “it is not *her* will, this thing that she wills; rather, it is the **will of God** that is everything she wills. For this soul does not take the lead in love, in a way that would make her follow her own will through any personal desire; instead, Love leads within her—Love has taken her will, and Love carries out his own will through her.”

Now Love works in her without her own effort, so that no <term>dis-ease</term><note>dis-ease: In this mystical context, it refers to inner turmoil, spiritual unrest, or the "unease" of the ego.</note> may dwell within her.

“Truly, Love,” says Reason, “these souls that become free in this way have known for many a day what it is like to be under the control of others. ## CHAPTER VI

### HOW THESE FREE SOULS HAVE NO WILL OF THEIR OWN, AND WHAT THEIR CONSTANT STATE IS

If anyone asks these free souls, who are so secure and peaceful, if they would want to be in <term>purgatory</term><note>In medieval theology, a place of purification where souls suffer for their sins before entering heaven.</note>, they say, "No." If they wish to be certain of their salvation while they are still living? They say, "No." If they wish to be in Paradise? They say, "No." 

"Wait! What then do they want?" 

They have no will at all to want these things; if they did want them, they would fall away from Love. For He who *is* <note>original: "he that is". A reference to God, often identified by the name "I Am" in mystical tradition.</note> possesses their will; He knows what is good for them, and that is enough for them, without them needing to know it or feel certain of it. 

"These souls," says Love, "live by the knowledge of love and by listening." This is the constant state of these souls, and they never depart from it; for knowledge, love, and the magnifying of God dwell within them. Souls such as these can find neither "good" nor "evil" in themselves, nor do they have enough self-consciousness to judge whether they are "converted" <note>Turned toward God.</note> or "perverted" <note>Turned away from God. Porete suggests the soul is so lost in God that it no longer examines its own spiritual status.</note>.

<summary>Love explains that the "Free Soul" has abandoned all personal desire, even the desire for heaven or salvation, leaving all things to God's will. These souls live in a state of constant peace, no longer judging themselves or worrying about their own spiritual standing.</summary>

## CHAPTER IX

->OF THE FIRST POINT SPOKEN OF BEFORE,<-
->CONCERNING THE SOUL IN THE ANNIHILATED LIFE; HOW<-

This soul knows only one thing about herself: that she is the root of all evil and the source of countless sins—sins without number, weight, or measure. She recognizes that sin is nothing, even less than nothing, and that a hundred horrible faults are worth even less than that. Through this understanding, she is "naughted" <term>naughted: a central concept in this text, referring to a mystical state of self-annihilation where the soul's ego is reduced to "nothing" (naught) so that God can act through them perfectly.</term> in relation to her own nature.

By her own honest judgment, she feels this would be true even if God were to take vengeance for only one in a thousand of her faults. This humility is the only true humility and the only true progress for a soul that has been "naughted."

# CHAPTER XVIII

## HOW THIS SOUL GIVES TO NATURE ALL THAT IT ASKS WITHOUT ANY STING OF CONSCIENCE, AND THE MEANING OF THIS

This soul gives to nature all that it asks for without any sting of conscience, because all **covetousness** <note>The original manuscript uses the term "properties," likely a translation of the Old French *propriété*. In this spiritual context, it refers to "self-love" or a spirit of proprietorship—the ego's desire to possess things for itself. This concept is central to the writer's theology of "nothingness."</note> of nature is dead in these creatures; and therefore the law of our Lord Jesus Christ is enclosed within such a life, and the divine gifts are above this law. 

"It is the truth," says Love, "that this soul does not place so much value or love on temporary things that she would gain anything by refusing nature's requests; why then should she make it a matter of conscience to give nature what is its due? But such a nature is so well-ordered by its union with divine love, to which the will of this soul is joined, that she asks for nothing that goes against the decree of divine righteousness. But these creatures are so excellent that men dare not speak openly or specifically of their ways, because of the...

<note>The text here references the idea that a perfected soul is so aligned with God's will that its "natural" desires are no longer selfish, but perfectly in tune with divine order. This was a controversial point in the Middle Ages, as it could be misinterpreted as an excuse for hedonism.</note>

“But she is humbled,” says Love, “by the knowledge of her own poverty—the nothingness she has of herself—so much so that it seems to her like a public humiliation <margin>The original manuscript uses the word "embaschement," meaning a state of being abashed or lowered.</margin> before the whole world, just as it is to her own inmost being. <margin>Or, "that it is to all the world a humiliation, as it is to her inmost being."</margin> And she is also intoxicated by the knowledge of the divine goodness, granted by the pure grace of the Godhead, which keeps her in a state of constant spiritual drunkenness. Beholding this goodness, she is filled with praise and the hearing of divine love; she is not drunk because of what she has already tasted, but she is truly drunk, and even more drunk, because of that which she has never drunk and never shall drink.” <margin>This mystical state arises not just from what the soul has experienced of divine love, but from her awareness of the infinite nature of God. She is intoxicated by the sheer potential of the Trinity’s love, which is so vast it can never be fully "consumed" by a creature.</margin>

“Ah, for God’s sake, Love,” says Reason, “what does this mean? How can this soul be drunk on what she has never drunk and will never drink?”

## CHAPTER IV

### HOW CONSOLATIONS THAT COMFORT SOULS THROUGH SWEET FEELINGS DO NOT BENEFIT THE SOUL, BUT ONLY THE MEDITATION OF PURE LOVE; AND HOW THAT MEDITATION HAS ONLY ONE MEANING, AND WHAT THAT MEANING IS

> "Now understand the rest, you lords who hear and lords who love! <note>The author addresses the audience as "lords," implying a spiritual nobility or those advanced in the contemplative life.</note> Understand this through a meditation of love that occurs without hearing anything from created beings—a meditation that souls receive in love without desiring any of God's gifts. These gifts are what people call <term>consolations</term> <note>Emotional or sensory feelings of "sweetness" or joy during prayer which were often considered a reward or sign of progress in medieval spirituality.</note> which comfort souls through a feeling of sweetness in prayer. Neither these feelings nor any other spiritual practices teach the soul; only pure love does. For whoever seeks the comforts of God through feelings of consolation lowers the value of <term>fine love</term>. <note>Derived from the courtly love tradition ("fin'amor"), here it refers to a high, purified spiritual love that is entirely selfless and seeks no personal gain, not even spiritual pleasure.</note>

<summary>This page argues that a truly advanced soul must move beyond "consolations"—the pleasant emotional feelings found in prayer—to reach a state of "fine love" that seeks God alone without desiring any personal reward.</summary>

## CHAPTER V

# CHAPTER VI

## WHAT IT MEANS THAT THIS SOUL DOES NOTHING AGAINST THE PEACE OF HER INNER BEING, AND AN EXAMPLE OF THIS

“**O LADY LOVE**,” <note>In this allegorical dialogue, "Love" represents the divine perspective, while "Reason" represents human logic, which often struggles to understand mystical experience.</note> says Reason, “explain to us what you mean by this: that the soul is in her true freedom of pure, clean love when she does nothing that goes against the peace her inner being requires?”

Does he do anything...”

## A COMPLAINT OF THIS SOUL, AND OF THE COMFORT THAT LOVE GIVETH HER, AND HOW SHE IS NOT SUFFICED NOR APPEASED IN THAT WHICH LOVE TELLETH HER, BUT WHEREIN SHE IS SUFFICED, COMFORTED, AND APPEASED; AND WHEREIN SHE HATH THE FULL SUBSTANCE OF HER DEMANDS

## CHAPTER II

### HOW GOD HAS LOVED THIS SOUL WITHOUT BEGINNING AND SHALL WITHOUT END; AND OF THE OBEDIENCE OF REASON TO THIS SOUL; AND OF THE HARMONY OF THE WILL OF GOD AND OF THIS SOUL; AND OF HER PEACE AND OF PERFECT CHARITY; AND OF THE REPROACHES OF CONSCIENCE <note>Marguerite Porete’s "Mirror" describes the journey of the "Annulled Soul" which, through Love, moves beyond the restrictive demands of Reason and Conscience.</note>

# CHAPTER 11
## CONCERNING THE UNION OF LOVE

This soul is imprinted in God; she has taken his very image through the union of love, in the same way that wax takes the form of a seal. In this way, this soul has taken the imprint of God and his very likeness. <note>The metaphor of wax and a seal was a common medieval illustration for how the soul, softened by love, can be reshaped to match the character of God.</note>
   This soul speaks in this way: “However well God loves me—as he has shown through his divine work and the suffering of his humanity <note>original: "manhood," referring to the physical life and crucifixion of Jesus</note>—he does not love me,” says this soul, “against himself. <note>This difficult phrase suggests that God’s love for an individual never contradicts his own divine nature, justice, or truth.</note> Even though he died for everyone and took on the flesh and blood of mankind, this was to bear witness to his goodness <note>original: "bounty"</note>, for he owed this to me since his Divine Will desired it. Because of this,” says this soul, “he does not love me against himself; for even though all those whom the Trinity created in its knowledge might have been damned without end, Jesus Christ, the Son of God the Father, has not, in truth, granted salvation to everyone.” <note>The author is touching on a complex theological point: while Christ’s sacrifice was offered for all, not all souls are saved, highlighting the mystery of divine justice and human will.</note>

which you grant to them more than to the perished?”

> “Where is it?” says Love. “They do indeed possess a state of being, and a very good state of being at that, in order to arrive at the highest state of being of which we speak—a state for which the perished can find no help.”

**M.** This word “perished” should not be understood as the destruction of the soul through damnation <note>original: "perdition"</note>, as though they would not be saved. Rather, it means—just as Love says—that they rely so much on their own good works, believing this to be the best path, that they continue to follow nothing else. Consequently, they cannot reach the highest state; for the sake of the lesser [virtues], they lose the best [union]. Therefore, the author calls them “perished,” not because of the works themselves, but because of the satisfaction they take in them. **N.** <note>The initials M. and N. likely refer to "M.N.," the anonymous medieval translator who added explanatory glosses to the original text to ensure its orthodoxy.</note>

## CHAPTER II

### WHAT POWER THE FREEDOM OF LOVE HAS, AND WHAT MAKES THIS SOUL MOST JOYFUL

This <term>creature</term> <note>original: "creature"; here referring to the human soul as a created being.</note> is naked, yet she is clothed with the life of glory of which we have spoken. Furthermore, she is naked of her body; just as an animal's skin is stripped of physical clothing, so too is her spirit stripped of her body. Thus, her spirit does not truly dwell within the body, for her body’s <term>sensuality</term> <note>original: "sensuality"; the faculty of the soul that experiences physical sensations and worldly desires.</note> has been worn away and set free by divine works. Consequently, this soul is naked and resides in that sweet, unknown country more truly than she resides in her own physical body where she gives life; such is the power that comes from the freedom of love.

Just so, all such words must be interpreted within themselves by those who read this book. For regarding these "dark" <note>Meaning obscure, veiled, or difficult to understand.</note> words and high matters spoken of unclearly in this writing, this is done to encourage the souls of readers who are inclined toward <term>ghostly feelings</term> <note>Spiritual insights or mystical experiences.</note> to circle around and <term>ensearch</term> <note>To search out, investigate, or examine deeply.</note> through subtle reasoning. The word "usage" means sometimes the habitual practices of devotion at any one point of the soul's development, and sometimes the condition itself, "a divine usage," as implying God's own act in the soul.

# CHAPTER X

## CONCERNING MARY MAGDALEN, ST. PETER, AND ST. JOHN, AND HOW GOD STILL WORKS IN SOULS AS HE DID IN THEM, IF THEY PREPARE THEMSELVES FOR IT

“Oh, for God’s sake, look at the sinful, repentant Magdalen: what shame or glory did she have when God said of her that she had chosen the better and most certain part <note>A reference to Luke 10:42, where Jesus tells Martha that Mary "has chosen the better part" (Latin: *optimam partem*), traditionally interpreted as the contemplative life.</note>, and when her Beloved said it should never be taken from her? <insert>[What shame did she feel]</insert> regarding the fact that her sins are known to all the people through such witnesses as the Evangelists? ## CHAPTER III

### HOW THESE SOULS ARE NEVER FEEBLE NOR BURDENED BY THEMSELVES

"O God," says **Reason**, "what beings these souls are! Truly, through baptism, they are never clearly weak," <margin>The original manuscript reads: "Truly at baptism clearly they are never feeble."</margin> says Reason, "nor burdened by themselves."

## CHAPTER VIII

### OF FOUR TREASURES <note>original: "costs." In this context, a "cost" refers to a valuable quality, condition, or price paid for a specific status.</note> THROUGH WHICH THIS SOUL IS MADE FREE; HOW SHE HAS LOST HER NAME BY THE UNION OF LOVE AND IS TURNED TOWARD LOVE, AND HOW THERE IS YET SOMETHING HIGHER THAN THIS; AND HOW NONE MAY UNDERSTAND THIS BOOK EXCEPT THOSE FOR WHOM LOVE HAS WRITTEN IT.

A servant <term>bondman</term> must possess four treasures before he can be set free and called a nobleman <term>gentleman</term> <note>In the Middle Ages, a "gentleman" was a person of noble birth and character, distinguished from a "bondman" or serf who was tied to the land.</note>; and it is exactly the same in the understanding of this spiritual practice.

Understand this, you who hear it, if you can! How might Love follow this practice regarding all the works of virtue, since human effort ceases when Love takes over? <note>The author suggests that at this high level of spiritual maturity, the soul's actions are so aligned with God that it no longer needs to consciously "strive" to be virtuous; virtue becomes its natural state.</note>

The second treasure is that she has no will of her own—any more than the dead in their graves—but only the divine will of God. This soul takes no heed of, nor does she have a heart for, righteousness, <note>This does not mean the soul is unrighteous, but that it is no longer preoccupied with its own "score" of good deeds, having surrendered entirely to God's will.</note>

[The soul has transitioned from] **Virtues** into **Love**; and from **Love** into **Naught**, and from **Naught** into the illuminations <note>original: "clarifyings"; referring to the process of divine enlightenment</note> of God, who sees with the eyes of his majesty. The total, singular loneliness of his own being gives her that state, which is the most noble existence any creature may have in this life of perfection.

This sixth state is the most profitable, the best, the most noble, and the most gentle of all.

# DIVISION X
## CHAPTER I
### CONCERNING THREE SIGNS BY WHICH IT MAY BE KNOWN THAT THE SOUL HAS NOT ATTAINED PEACE, BUT IS STILL BEGGING; AND WHAT PARADISE IS

O God, who can do all things; O Lord, who knows all things; O my Beloved, who is sufficient for all, do whatever You will. Sweet Father, I have no power! Sweet Master, I have no knowledge! Sweet Beloved, I am nothing. And therefore, I desire nothing. 

And if anyone says, "Ah, for God's sake, let us allow nothing of our own, nor of anyone else besides Him, to remain within us from now on—which God, in His goodness, must drive out"—this person is a <term>begging creature</term> <note>In Porete’s theology, a "begging creature" is a soul that is still trying to reach God through its own efforts, virtues, or desires, rather than being completely "naughted" or emptied of self-will.</note>, who through her own sense of emptiness seeks God among created things. Truly, she finds the result that she desires and that she herself brings about. <note>She finds what she seeks, and by her own activity procures the spiritual consolation she desires, and does the work herself; but it is not *God* whom she reaches.</note> But truly, the soul that finds Him allows Him to do His will and His divine works within her, without her own...

## CHAPTER II

# DIVISION XII

## THE ONLY CHAPTER

### HOW THOSE WHO POSSESS SOVEREIGNTY OVER ALL THINGS KNOW AND FEEL THE LIFE OF WHICH THIS BOOK SPEAKS, AND NO ONE ELSE BUT THEM

AMONG you ladies to whom God has given this life from His **divine bounty** <term>divine bounty: God's limitless generosity and grace</term> in abundance, without holding anything back—not only this life alone that we are discussing, but another life alongside it of which no man has ever spoken—you shall recognize your own spiritual **estate** <term>estate: one's spiritual condition or "rank" in the eyes of God</term> in this book. 

And those who are not in this state, nor ever were, nor ever shall be, do not feel this way of being. They do not know it, nor can they, nor will they, for they do not belong to the **lineage** <term>lineage: a spiritual family or ancestry of souls who share the same divine nature</term> of which we speak. 

Truly, know this to be true! For even the angels of the first order are not **Seraphim** <term>Seraphim: the highest rank of angels, traditionally associated with fire and the most intense love for God</term>, nor can they ever be, because God did not grant them the nature of Seraphim. They feel it through the strength of the lineage to which they belong, and through which they shall become even stronger than they are now.

But the righteous man keeps himself from consenting to the fault—a fault which might otherwise grow because of that inclination. Thus, his "falling" (that tendency toward error mentioned before) is actually more of a virtue to him than a vice. This is because his will remains free by rejecting the fault, as was said before. Now you may understand how the righteous man falls from a high state to a low one, and how that falling, though it is "low," is more virtue than vice.

“Now understand: since it is so that the righteous man falls seven times a day, then it must be that he rises seven times—otherwise he could not rise from those seven falls! Now we have a will coming out of his bounty and out of his power, so that we may be more free—just as he has a will out of his power and his own unique freedom <note>This passage reflects the author’s training in the traditions of St. Augustine, emphasizing that human freedom is a derivative of God's absolute freedom.</note>. 

And the divine goodness saw that we were on the path to destruction and ruin <note>original: "pestilence and perdition"</note> because of the free will that he had given us. Yet this will came out of his goodness and it was given to us by his grace. Thus was human nature **joined** <note>original: "knit"</note> to divine goodness in the person of the Son, in order to pay the ransom of our debts that we have committed by our sinful will. Now I may see by this where I ought to be: namely, that I should return to where I was, in that same point where I existed within **the One** <note>The "One" refers to the Neoplatonic and mystical concept of God as the singular, undifferentiated source of all being. The soul seeks to return to its state before it was "created" as a separate entity.</note>. And that I should be so beloved by him, even as he is 'He Who Is'; and as naked as I was when..."

<summary>This page explains that human free will is a gift from God's "Uncreated Goodness" and that Christ's incarnation was necessary to redeem the misuse of that will. The soul's ultimate goal is to return to its original, "naked" state of union within the divine One.</summary>

# CHAPTER X

## HOW WE MUST DRAW WITHIN OURSELVES THE WHOLE LIFE THAT OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST HIMSELF LIVED AND PREACHED, ACCORDING TO OUR ABILITY; AND THE GOAL WE SHALL REACH THROUGH IT

<margin>f 275</margin>
**THIS** book shows through <term>partial thoughts</term> <note>original: "thoughts of partie"; this refers to fragmented, individual concerns or specific virtues that belong to the "active life" rather than the "whole" or divine unity.</note>, through works of perfection, and through the requirements of reason, that it is necessary for us to draw into ourselves the whole life that Jesus Christ himself lived and preached to us, as far as we are able. For this state to be within us is true Being.

# CHAPTER XI

## WHETHER A CREATURE MAY DWELL IN LIFE AND BE ALWAYS OUTSIDE OF HERSELF. AND WHEN A SOUL IS OUTSIDE OF HERSELF, AND WHAT SHE LIVES UPON WHEN SHE IS WITHOUT HERSELF

I ask of <term>clarified</term> <note>meaning souls purified from earthly attachments</note> and <term>enlumined</term> <note>meaning souls enlightened by divine wisdom</note> souls—who live differently than those previously named—if any human creature can remain in this life and always be “*outside*” <note>original: "without"; in this context, it means "beyond" or "outside" of one's own ego and self-will</note> themselves? If these two cannot tell me, no one shall, for no one knows it unless they belong to this spiritual lineage. Truth speaks for them in response to our questioning, and Love declares it; they say that a soul is then <term>naughted</term> <note>original: "naughted"; a technical term in medieval mysticism referring to the process of the soul becoming "nothing" so that God can be "everything" within it</note> “*outside*” herself when she has no natural impulses, no inner spiritual labor, no shame, no desire for honor, no fear of anything that might happen, and no personal affections. The Divine Goodness is no longer received through the human Will, but is present at all times without the soul's own willing. And then this soul is brought to nothingness by a spiritual height beyond herself—that is, the reality that God alone is enough for her. Then she does everything outside of herself. And if she does everything outside of herself, is it any wonder that she no longer exists for her own sake?

## CHAPTER II
### CONCERNING THE SECOND STATE, WHICH IS FOLLOWING THE COUNSEL THAT OUR LORD GAVE TO REACH PERFECTION

“THE second <term>state</term> <note>or stage of spiritual being</note> is that a soul observes what God counsels to His special lovers, going beyond that which He commands. ## CHAPTER IV

-> VOCABULARY <-

**Fourth State**: The stage of spiritual resting.
**Contemplation**: Experiencing God's presence without active thought.
**Meditation**: Active reflection on spiritual truths.
**Dangerous**: Spiritually fastidious or unapproachable by the world.
**Gladsome**: Filled with spiritual joy.
**Privities**: The secret inner workings of the heart.
**Union**: The state of becoming one with God.
**Lordship**: Mastery or possession of a spiritual state.
**Simple Souls**: The "Free Souls" who have moved beyond the need for religious rules.

In this state, the soul feels such intense joy and union with God that she believes no higher spiritual experience could possibly exist.</summary>

## CHAPTER II

# DIVISION XX

## CHAPTER I

### HOW THIS SOUL IS IN HER HIGHEST PERFECTION WHEN HOLY CHURCH TAKES NO EXAMPLE FROM HER. AND WHAT HOLY CHURCH IS. AND OF THREE THINGS THAT CAUSE THIS SOUL TO HAVE NO FEAR.

"**T**his soul," says Love, "is in her highest perfection and closest to the far-near <note>The OCR reads "far night," but in the context of this mystical tradition, it refers to the 'Far-Near'—a name for God who is transcendentally distant yet intimately present.</note> when Holy Church takes no notice of her life <note>original: "taketh not of ensample." This means the soul's spiritual life is so elevated that it no longer fits the standard models or "examples" used by the institutional Church.</note>. She is then within the work of purity <note>original: "cleanness."</note>, and above the work of charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the active performance of virtuous deeds, which the soul has transcended in favor of a state of pure being.</note>. She is so far removed from the works of virtue that she can no longer even understand their language.

But the works of the virtues are all enclosed within this soul, and they obey her without any resistance. And because they are so enclosed, Holy Church cannot recognize her; here, 'Holy Church' refers specifically to the <term>fear of God</term> <note>original: "dread of God."</note>, for holy fear is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. And yet, nevertheless, the fear of God might disturb the state of spiritual <term>freedom</term> <note>original: "freeness."</note>."

<summary>Love explains that a soul in its highest perfection transcends the active practice of virtues and the institutional "fear of God." Because the soul has internalized all virtue, she moves into a state of spiritual freedom that the standard Church cannot fully comprehend.</summary>

## CHAPTER II
### CONCERNING THE WORTHINESS OF GOD’S BOUNTY AND THE UNION IT CREATES BETWEEN GOD AND THIS SOUL

BOUNTY <term>Divine Generosity</term> <note>original: "Bounty." In this mystical context, it refers to God’s infinite, overflowing goodness and grace that exists independently of human effort.</note> is worth more than all the works that any creature might perform in a hundred thousand years, or even all the works of the Holy Church. The furthest part of this is actually the closest, for it unites <note>original: "oneth." A Middle English term meaning "to make one" or "to unify."</note> this being from within himself, and it causes the soul to always be knit to his will, without ever being moved from it, no matter what might happen to her. 

All things are one to her, without fear and without joy, for she is no longer an individual person within this Oneness. At that point, she has no more to do with God than God has to do with her, for he **is** and she **is not**. She has held nothing back in the **naughting** <term>annihilation</term> <note>The "naughted" soul is one that has been emptied of self-will and individual identity to the point of becoming "nothing," allowing God to be everything within her.</note> of herself; it is enough for her that He exists. And she does not exist; for she is without a separate being, existing in that state where she was before she was created <note>original: "there where she was, ere she was not." This refers to the soul's eternal existence as an idea in the mind of God before its physical creation.</note>. Thus she receives from God that which she has; and she is what God is, through the union of love, at that very point where she existed before God had created her out of his bounty.

# NOTES

## NOTE 2, page 14.

<term>M. N.</term> <note>The initials used by the anonymous 14th-century English translator who added explanatory notes to Marguerite Porete’s text to ensure it was interpreted in a religiously "safe" or orthodox way.</note> interprets the mystic in the light of <term>moral theology</term> <note>The study of how humans should act to live a virtuous life according to divine law.</note>, and supplies the <term>ascetical</term> <note>Relating to self-discipline and the active pursuit of virtue through effort.</note> basis of the author’s more <term>transcendent doctrines</term> <note>Teachings that describe a spiritual state beyond ordinary human experience or effort.</note>. Possibly **X** (the author) <note>Referring to Marguerite Porete, the author of the original work.</note> presupposed this explanation of growth in the conquest of virtue, but she seems also to have had in mind the theory, developed further on in the book, namely, that the soul when liberated by **Love** becomes free from the anxious preoccupation concerning **Virtue** and—being, of course, in grace and habitually pursuing virtue—finds her attention focused directly upon the contemplation of God’s love. 

In proportion as she grows in union, her self-consciousness diminishes. As the revelation of God to the soul progresses, so the soul becomes more passive <note>In this context, "passive" means "receptive," where the soul stops trying to "do" things and instead allows God to work within it.</note>, both with regard to effort after virtue and search for knowledge. These increase steadily by God’s work in the soul, but there is ever less and less self-consciousness concerning these things.

The constantly growing factor, the hunger and thirst after God, supplies the right <term>affective impetus</term> <note>The emotional and spiritual drive or "longing" that moves the soul toward God.</note>, which, in the earlier stages, was known—and to some extent remains always—as a desire for personal holiness and a knowledge of God.

The affective element outlasts the other personal elements, but is itself purified in the “far night” of <term>aridity</term> <note>A term in mysticism for "spiritual dryness," a period where a person feels no comfort, joy, or emotional connection to God during prayer, often seen as a stage of deep purification.</note>, and is later realized as being but the last human trappings of self behind which the “**Spirit of God**” resides in that part of the soul completely inaccessible to self-consciousness.

***

**Key Terms Found in this Section:**
*   **Moral theology:** The study of religious ethics and virtue.
*   **Ascetical basis:** The foundation of spiritual life built on self-denial and discipline.
*   **Transcendent doctrines:** Advanced spiritual teachings on the soul's union with the Divine.
*   **Virtue:** Moral excellence and righteousness.
*   **Contemplation:** A deep, quiet focus on God beyond words or images.
*   **Self-consciousness:** An awareness of one's own self and actions, which the mystic seeks to lose in God.
*   **Affective impetus:** The power of the heart's longing or love.
*   **Aridity:** A painful but purifying period of spiritual emptiness.
*   **Mysticism:** The pursuit of direct, personal experience of the Divine.

# NOTES

## Note 2, p. 24.

> “*For sin must be had in conscience.*” This does not mean that sin is merely a matter of subjective <term>conscience</term> <note>In this context, the internal moral judgment or awareness of right and wrong.</note>, and that by directing his intention aright a man delivers himself from responsibility for fleshly sin. Rather, assuming freedom from the grosser sins and progress in the <term>spiritual life</term>, infirmities, frailties, even <term>venial sins</term> <note>Less serious sins that do not completely separate the soul from God's grace, unlike "mortal" sins.</note>, are not to be overemphasized, and in this state no sin is committed without the deliberate consent of conscience: “Sin must be had in conscience.”

If the conscience is directed wholly towards God, the soul enjoys a freedom of spirit in which the lawful demands of nature can now be legitimately satisfied without fear of impulses to excess, and without need of the constant check of violent <term>mortification</term> <note>The practice of self-discipline or physical self-denial intended to strengthen the spirit and overcome worldly desires.</note>. But at no stage of the spiritual life does the soul find itself able to give up watchfulness nor to abandon all deliberate mortification.

> “*Will a man or nil he so, in the time after.*” Frailties committed by surprise, not by consent of conscience and repudiated, at the time or after, by the will, are not necessarily sins. But such actions, though unintended, can become sinful by a return of evil desire to which the heart yields itself.

## Note 1, p. 104.

This qualifying statement together with others are according to the doctrine of <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>original: "Dionysius Areopagita"; a 5th-century Christian theologian whose writings on mystical union and the nature of God were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>. They save the treatise from the errors of <term>Pantheism</term> <note>The belief that God is identical with the universe or that the soul becomes identical in substance with God.</note> and of <term>Quietism</term> <note>A mystical movement that emphasized a state of perfect passivity, which critics feared could lead to the abandonment of moral effort or the sacraments.</note>. The author guards against the Pantheistic theory that the soul can be so absorbed into the divine nature as to become identical with it. “Not by nature divine.” “The treasure fulfilled which is in the <term>Trinity</term>” <note>The Christian doctrine of God existing as one being in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> becomes the property of the soul by the active and constantly

It also highlights the influence of Dionysius the Areopagite in ensuring the text remains within orthodox boundaries regarding the relationship between the soul and the Trinity.</summary>

There is never identification of nature <note>The author clarifies that while the soul may be united with God, it never actually becomes God in essence; the distinction between the Creator and the created remains.</note>. Furthermore, the states of indifference and unknowing, which are described, are not <term>quietistic passivity</term> <note>A reference to "Quietism," a controversial mystical movement that suggested a person should be completely still and stop all effort to reach God; the author here argues that the soul is actually very active, just in a way that the physical senses cannot perceive.</note>. The author insists on the interior spiritual activity inaccessible to the senses, and therefore indescribable, but issuing in the soul’s possession of the treasure “enclosed in the Trinity.”

->Note 3, p. 105.<-

The division of souls into two classes, those guided by Reason, and those led by Love—*i.e.*, <term>rationalism</term> *v.* <term>mysticism</term>—is a very old and a very modern concept. The author makes a bold personification here, definitely subordinating the former family to the latter; “Holy Church the little, or less, or Holy-Church-under-*The* Holy Church” <note>This refers to the "Little Church" of the institutional hierarchy and human logic, which is seen as inferior to the "Great Church" of souls who are in direct, mystical union with God.</note>.

No heresy is intended, such as the <term>Jansenist</term> <note>A 17th-century theological movement within Catholicism that was eventually condemned for its extreme views on predestination and the idea that only a few "elect" people receive God's grace.</note> theory of the “elect,” but merely a statement of the probable relation in which “Rationalising Reason” and “Intuitive Love” stand to each other. The bold humour of the passage is intensified and preserved from unpleasantness by Holy-Church-the-little’s acceptance of the stricture <note>A "stricture" is a piece of criticism or a restriction.</note>.

The key to the situation is indicated in the fact that she “praises them in the <term>glosses</term> <note>Explanatory notes or interpretations written in the margins of a book to explain the meaning of the main text.</note> of our scriptures.” The “glossing of the scriptures” is one of the true functions for the “rationalistic” faculties.

->Note 2, p. 205.<-

# NOTES

Perfection is only thwarted when the soul goes unbidden in this “search of the virtues” <note>The author suggests that seeking spiritual perfection through one's own effort or willpower, rather than waiting for God's invitation, actually hinders the soul’s progress.</note>.

It is not the soul itself which feels—only the surface regions are affected—“this is not she.” Cf. St Francis de Sales’s teaching <note>Saint Francis de Sales (1567–1622) taught that the "fine point" or the very center of the spirit remains in peace even when the lower emotions or the "surface" of the mind are in turmoil.</note>.

In this and the following chapters we must distinguish those who are “in life of spirit”—i.e., souls who have passed through the life of the “perished” and of the “marred” states—but who have not attained to the life of the “free souls” <note>In Porete's system, the soul must first die to its own desires ("perished") and its own will ("marred") before it can become a "free soul" acting purely by God's love.</note>.

### Note 1, p. 241.

“*Thoughts of <term>partie</term>*” <note>original: "partie"</note>. A **partie** is a game in which a subject is discussed from two or more points of view. In the courts of love of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, subjects were thus debated and poems—*jeu-partis* <note>original: "jeu-partis"; translated as "debate-games" or "divided-games," a form of Old French lyric poetry.</note>—presented for prize competitions.

The meaning here seems to be “by thoughts framed in dialogue,” but below, “in putting out,” etc. “by avoiding all discursive meditation <note>Discursive meditation refers to the process of using the intellect and imagination to think through religious scenes or logical arguments, as opposed to the quiet, wordless state of contemplation.</note>, all dwelling on particular points of prayer.”

### Note 1, p. 251.

St Bonaventure’s *The Soul's Journey into God* <note>original: "Itinerarium Mentis [in Deum]"</note> describes seven stages by which the mind ascends to God. The first three deal with the corporeal nature of the senses, imagination, and the rational soul of man. The fourth to the seventh show the supernatural intervention of grace by the help of which we see God revealed in his Being (4), in his goodness (5), and in the mystery of the Trinity (6). The seventh stage is the repose of ecstasy.

# NOTES

It is evident that this system has influenced the author of the *Mirror* (see Division XIV, chaps. 6 and 7); it represents the reaction of pluralistic mysticism <note>A type of mysticism that emphasizes the distinctness of the individual soul even in its union with God, rather than the soul being absorbed into a single substance.</note> against the theories of the twelfth-century revival of monistic philosophy and the mystics. The Franciscan school identifies the Beatific Vision <note>The ultimate, direct sight of God as He is, which constitutes the highest happiness in heaven.</note> with Love, and makes Love the method by which it is apprehended. Freedom in love is the keynote of Franciscan spirituality as it is of the *Mirror*. St Bernard did not hold that the Godhead is revealed to man by immediate intuition, but is known through species <note>original: "species"; in medieval philosophy, these are the mental images or representations through which the mind perceives reality, rather than seeing the essence of a thing directly.</note>.

Our author is more influenced by the “Seven Stages” of the Ascent to God in St Augustine’s *On the Magnitude of the Soul* <note>original: "De Quantitate Animae"; written by St. Augustine around 388 AD, this work describes the soul's progression through seven levels of power and spiritual growth.</note>, than by the treatise of Richard of St Victor <note>A 12th-century Scottish philosopher and mystic who outlined a six-stage path of contemplation in his works.</note>, who describes six stages of contemplation.

In the "courts of love" <note>Refers to a medieval cultural tradition, primarily in France, where aristocratic circles held formal debates on the nature of love and chivalry.</note> of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, subjects were thus debated and poems—debate-songs <note>original: "jeu-partis"; a poetic genre where two speakers debate a specific question, often used in competition.</note>—presented for prize competitions.

# EXTRA VOLUMES

*These are similar in character, format, and style to the rest of the series, but are issued at a lower price because their content is considerably shorter than that of the other volumes.*

**1ex. CERTAIN DEVOUT and GODLY PRAYERS, made in Latin by Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into English by Thomas Paynell, Clerk.** [*Published in 1925.*]

A little volume of great spiritual beauty, written by the famous Bishop and <term>Confessor for the Faith</term> <note>A title given to those who suffered for their religious beliefs but were not killed as martyrs</note>; reprinted from the only edition, published "at London, in St. Paul’s Churchyard, at the sign of the Holy Ghost, by John Cawood, Printer to the King’s and Queen’s Majesties, in the year 1558." <note>original: "at the synge of the Holye Ghoste... Anno 1558"</note>

> "Attractive in appearance and still more attractive in content, for the prayers are distinguished by depth of feeling and simplicity of expression."—*Catholic Gazette.*
> "The prayers breathe a spirit of deep humility and reverence. Paynell is excellent in his English rendering."—*Southern Cross.*
> "A charming little book."—*Month.*
> "No Catholic can open this little book without deep interest. . . . We hope that these and similar old English devotions may become even better known and more popular."—*Catholic Book Notes.*

**2ex. THE BLIND OBEDIENCE OF AN HUMBLE PENITENT, THE BEST CURE FOR SCRUPLES. By Sylvester Jenks, Bishop-Elect of Callipolis. With an Introduction by the Editor of the Series.** <note>Callipolis, or Gallipoli, was a "titular see," meaning Bishop Jenks held the title of the city even though it was no longer under Catholic administration</note> [*Published in 1925.*]

> "A really helpful work; although over two centuries have elapsed since it was first written, it is so well edited that, instead of appearing strange, it is quaint. It maintains interest at the same time as it gives spiritual instruction."—*Catholic Truth.*
> "Robust sense, a living faith and a fine humor make the little book pleasant and profitable."—*Southern Cross.*

**3ex. THE PRACTICE OF THE PRESENCE OF GOD. Being the Conversations, Letters and Spiritual Maxims of Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, <term>Discalced Carmelite</term> <note>A branch of the Carmelite order that emphasizes a more austere life of poverty, symbolized by being "discalced" or barefoot/wearing sandals</note>. Newly translated by Donald Attwater.** [*Published in 1926.*]

This little Catholic classic has previously been available in English only in non-Catholic versions.

<meta>This page presents the decorative frontispiece or bookplate design for "The Orchard Books" series, following the catalog of volumes described on the previous page. The design is a hallmark of the Arts and Crafts aesthetic applied to religious publishing.</meta>

->HOPE AMID EVILS<- <note>original: "Sperate Malis" (transcribed in OCR as "S Parate Malis"). This Latin motto, frequently used in the "Orchard Books" series, is an exhortation to maintain spiritual hope and resilience during times of adversity or "evils."</note>

P W <note>These are the initials of Philip Webb (1831–1915), a famous English architect and a founding member of the Arts and Crafts movement. He designed this specific "orchard" motif—featuring fruit trees and vines—to serve as the visual identity for this series of spiritual classics.</note>

<summary>This page displays the artistic frontispiece for the "Orchard Books" series, featuring a lush, decorative fruit-tree pattern and a Latin motto of hope designed by the influential artist Philip Webb.</summary>
<keywords>Philip Webb, Arts and Crafts movement, bookplate, Latin motto, Orchard Books, graphic design, woodcut style</keywords>

--- Page 387 ---
<meta>This page features the decorative endpaper design for the "Orchard Books" series, a collection of classic spiritual and devotional texts. This illustration follows the series catalog, serving as the visual signature for the volumes, and was created by the artist Paul Woodroffe (1875–1954).</meta>

<margin>P</margin> <note>The initial "P" stands for Paul, the first name of the illustrator Paul Woodroffe.</note>
<margin>W</margin> <note>The initial "W" stands for Woodroffe. He was a prominent member of the Arts and Crafts movement and a noted stained-glass artist.</note>

->ROOT OUT FROM EVILS<- <note>original: "EXTIRPATE DE MALIS." This Latin motto literally commands the reader to "root out" or "eradicate" themselves from evil. While similar to the series' other motto, *Sperate de Malis* (Hope amidst evils), this version uses a botanical pun—"extirpate" means to pull up by the roots—which perfectly matches the visual theme of the orchard and vines shown in the design.</note>
